cards.title: Java Deployment Archives: JAR vs WAR
cards.content:
In modern Java development, choosing how to package your application is the first step toward deployment.

  • JAR (Java Archive): Standard for microservices. Bundles classes, resources, and an embedded servlet container (like Tomcat in Spring Boot) into a single, executable file. Run via java -jar app.jar.
  • WAR (Web Archive): Legacy/Traditional standard. Requires a standalone web server or application server (like Tomcat, WildFly, or WebLogic) to run.

cards.title: Containerizing Java Applications
cards.content:
Dockerizing Java applications ensures consistency across development, testing, and production environments.

A modern production-grade Dockerfile uses a multi-stage build to keep the final image small:

# Stage 1: Build
FROM maven:3.8-openjdk-17 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Stage 2: Runtime
FROM openjdk:17-jdk-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/target/*.jar app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

cards.title: JVM Tuning and Container Awareness
cards.content:
Historically, Java applications inside containers did not recognize container memory limits, leading to sudden OS-level kills (OOM Killer).

Since Java 10+, the JVM is container-aware. However, explicit sizing is still recommended:

  • -Xms: Initial heap size.
  • -Xmx: Maximum heap size.
  • -XX:+UseG1GC: Enables the G1 Garbage Collector, recommended for multi-threaded server apps.

cards.title: CI/CD Pipelines for Java
cards.content:
Continuous Integration & Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) automates Java deployments.

A standard pipeline features the following stages:

  1. Checkout: Pull latest codebase from Git repository.
  2. Build & Test: Run tests using mvn clean test. Fail pipeline if tests break.
  3. Analyze: Check code quality (e.g., SonarQube) and search for vulnerabilities.
  4. Package: Build production artifact and upload image.
  5. Deploy: Rollout update to cloud environment.

cards.title: Blue-Green vs Canary Deployments
cards.content:
Minimizing downtime during release cycles requires reliable cutover strategies:

  • Blue-Green Deployment: Maintains two identical environments. Active traffic goes to "Blue". Deploy new code to "Green". Test on Green, then switch router/load balancer traffic instantly to Green.
  • Canary Deployment: Gradually route a small subset of production traffic (e.g., 5%) to the new version. If metrics remain healthy, scale traffic to 100%.

cards.title: Post-Deployment Monitoring & Health Checks
cards.content:
Once deployed, your application must report its condition continuously.

Using Spring Boot Actuator provides built-in endpoints:

  • /actuator/health: Confirms application availability for load balancers.
  • /actuator/metrics: Exposes internal telemetry metrics.

These metrics are typically scraped by Prometheus and displayed on Grafana dashboards.
